Title: [LSJ] Rules clarification needed: Play to Win and the new rules

Messages.Author: Nya
Messages.Body:
Hello,

During our last tournament appeared some problems with an
interpretation of the new rules.

Situation:

Player A (Menele combat + weenie dom support: bruise bleed) ->
Player B (Ravnos Tumnimos breed + sens.dep. & Edged Illusions) ->
Player C (Tupdog archetype) ->
Player D (big cap Lasombra combat)

During the first few round Tupdogs trampled the Ravnos and after
sending lonely Lasombra combatant they started finishing off their
prey.

"A" seeing it's chance was just pumping up blood and influencing dom
weenies with occasionally -almost-always-succesfull dom-bleeding.

Ravnos' player had to deal with tupdogs each turn to safe their minions
( "No aggressive actions towards Tupdogs - no combat entering" - with
initiative in Tupdogs turn).

In the meantime "C" have finished "D's" second big cap and had him
leveled down to 6 pool.

And now:

Players started to chat for a very long time trying to convince each
other to share VP's among each other. Offers were first launched by
Ravnos player "B" who had lowest chances for a single VP besides the
near dead "D". He offered 2-2 table split to his predator and then when
he refused, he offered same deal to his prey. "A" realized that the
situation is going in the wrong way for him and started to renew the
offer - and was offering VP's split to his prey and predator.

Situation was somehow funny because 2 players [without D of course]
have powers to sweep the third ( tupdog's enter combat, menele combat,
Edged Illusions and sensory) and the balance was on a clay legs.

Player "C" decided to deal with player "B" ( he said simply that
fighting with single Menele is less riskier than trying to kill all the
Ravnos before they launch their EI (which Ravnos' player was discarding
three in a row) and split the table 2-2

- they knew that the new rule will cause them to cancel the deal when
they'll be left to 1 on 1 - so they decided to finish the "D" and "A"
with constant self weakening by the "C" player (transfering, moving
blood from pool to V via the dools hunting with the rest etc; when "A"
was almost dead - "C" was tapped with only 2 minions and 2 VP's and the
ravnos finished him easily.

So in the end the VP's went as they wished

QUESTIONS:

.1) Was it legal ?

2) What have to do the judge and what he could do in such situation if
it's NOT legal?

3) Was it a violate of the "Play to Win" rule? Or other rules?

If the problem can't be solved with these informations about situation
- just please write some possibilities.

Thanks in advance for your help.

regards

Naia

> ..1) Was it legal ?

If it was play to win, sure. That's something for the judge on the the scene to
determine.

If C's self-weakening was PTW (with the deal in place), then it's legal for him
to self-weaken.

The B-C 2-2 deal is only legal if neither C nor B had a chance at the GW.

> 2) What have to do the judge and what he could do in such situation if
> it's NOT legal?

Stop the play that violates PTW.

> 3) Was it a violate of the "Play to Win" rule? Or other rules?

Hard to say. Seems unlikely that no one was in a position to get a GW.

The judge's

> If player is seeing his forthcoming demise
> and deals with predator with explained way is it still only judge to
> decide?

Yes.

> Even if he didn't see whole game?

The only history that would be interesting would be reflected in the present
game state (including the player's library, since it is assumed the player knows
what cards are in his library), so sure -- he doesn't have to witness the whole
game.

> And what about denying this
> deal by judge? He comes to the table saying we can't make this deal
> because in his opinion one of us can get GW. and then player who was
> denied making this deal is trampled by others because judge was wrong.

Not because the judge was wrong, but because the probabilities didn't work out
in his favor.

The judge doesn't have to step in and guarantee a winner. He just makes a
judgment as to whether someone is playing to win.

> 0 vp. A player had a good table view but it was denied by judge. If he
> could be allowed to make a deal he would achieve 2 vps so playing with
> PTW rule. Is it necessery to completly describe situation on the turn
> when the deal was made?

The deal can be made in any event. It just can't be used as an excuse to violate
PTW unless the deal itself is PTW.

So you only really have to check with the judge when the player attempts some
activity which is not PTW in itself. Probably better to call the judge when the
deal is being made, so the judge can work with the best information available.

The short answer is Yes. In the end, it's up to the judge's judgement,
but LSJ has defined "reasonable chance" to include risk analysis.
Therefore, the failure states matter.

Here is a good thread on PTW, which also links to the original thread
(as far as I know) where LSJ mentioned risk analysis as part of
"reasonable chance."

http://tinyurl.com/y3496t

It seems that the current tournament rules still allow very trustworthy
people to make and keep deals like the one you described, but it does
make it more risky to do. Therefore, those types of deals are
discouraged a bit more, which was a goal of the rules change.

Ira

Sort of.

The deal doesn't just hinge on *you* playing-to-win. The judge may
decide that you giving up a very risky GW is reasonable play on your
part, but is the *other* player giving up a much easier to gain GW?

Also, on a 4 player table, organising a 2-2 split is very hard. You
bleed your prey out twice (2VP), and then I oust you and get last man
standing (2VP). If we're cross-table, I can't think of an easy way to
do it these days (withdrawal is half a VP).

The problem is that when it's down to just the two of us, all deals are
off. So you have to try your hardest (with 12 extra pool, which is a
lot) to oust me. The problem in the stated example was that one player
was trying to get around this by intentionally weakening himself. In a
real, honest situation, you have to try to oust me and I have to try to
oust you.

Knowing that, at 2 players, all deals are off, I'd be foolish to make
that deal in the first place. It's very likely not a play-to-win deal,
because you get 2VP and I get nothing out of the deal.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <1168507605.7...@i39g2000hsf.googlegroups.com>,

olivier...@gmail.com writes:
>I don't understand how technicly you do a 2/2 deal?
>
>Each player kill his prey and then wath?

Potentially:

One player could, legitimately, find that he can oust his prey and
grand-prey but only if he implodes in the process. Then his predator
ousts him. This is much the same as the artificial deals, where a
player ousts two preys and then *pretends* to find themselves in
unimaginable difficulty, but without the pretending.

An example might be having to throw all your vampires at a prey who is a
big wall. Some of your vampires get through, but most of them get
creamed. By the time you have the pool to bring out new vampires (after
the oust), it's too late for you to bring out a new vampire (who might
be very big, say) without your predator ousting you. Had you not agreed
to this course of action, your predator would have ousted you (but then
been blocked by the wall herself).

Though all deals would be off once you were down to two players, you
would have legitimately improved your standing (2VP rather than zero),
and your predator has too (2VP rather than one, when it hit the wall).

This would not necessarily have to be a deal. The predator could say
"Look, if you don't throw yourself at your prey, I'm just going to oust
you right now, and you'll have nothing. Might as well try?" I've
certainly seen players control their prey in such a fashion, when they
have absolute domination of their prey, but would be creamed by the next
one. At this point, it's just strategically good play, potentially.

One such example involved a three-player end-game, where a Ravnos weenie
breed deck had convinced its prey it was holding Week of Nightmares
(which it was), aided by the fact that the prey had seen a similar deck
in action before from the same player. Had the prey not gone along with
the requests, it would have been ousted the following turn with a swarm
of +1 bleeds. The Ravnos deck could then have got through with only one
turn of blocking to deal with (damaging a number of vampires), rather
than having that happen twice (which would have caused rather more
damage). So they prey hung on and did what he was told, in order to try
to get the scraps.
